inputs.instruction:
Please convert this command to run for the Slurm Workload manager on AWS Parallel Compute Service.
The cluster will have the Elastic Fabric Adapter for low latency networking, running on hpc7g.6xlarge.
These details have no implications for the Slurm directives, they are for your FYI.

Since we are converting to Slurm (with more flags and options) you MUST try to write the command to IMPROVE performance.
Please add comments to the sbatch script about what you did and why.
Here are directives for Slurm:
Usage: sbatch [OPTIONS(0)...] [ : [OPTIONS(N)...]] script(0) [args(0)...]

Parallel run options:
  -a, --array=indexes         job array index values
  -A, --account=name          charge job to specified account
      --bb=<spec>             burst buffer specifications
      --bbf=<file_name>       burst buffer specification file
  -b, --begin=time            defer job until HH:MM MM/DD/YY
      --comment=name          arbitrary comment
      --cpu-freq=min[-max[:gov]] requested cpu frequency (and governor)
  -c, --cpus-per-task=ncpus   number of cpus required per task
  -d, --dependency=type:jobid[:time] defer job until condition on jobid is satisfied
      --deadline=time         remove the job if no ending possible before
                              this deadline (start > (deadline - time[-min]))
      --delay-boot=mins       delay boot for desired node features
  -D, --chdir=directory       set working directory for batch script
  -e, --error=err             file for batch script's standard error
      --export[=names]        specify environment variables to export
      --export-file=file|fd   specify environment variables file or file
                              descriptor to export
      --get-user-env          load environment from local cluster
      --gid=group_id          group ID to run job as (user root only)
      --gres=list             required generic resources per node
      --gres-flags=opts       flags related to GRES management
  -H, --hold                  submit job in held state
      --ignore-pbs            Ignore #PBS and #BSUB options in the batch script
  -i, --input=in              file for batch script's standard input
  -J, --job-name=jobname      name of job
  -k, --no-kill               do not kill job on node failure
  -L, --licenses=names        required license, comma separated
  -M, --clusters=names        Comma separated list of clusters to issue
                              commands to.  Default is current cluster.
                              Name of 'all' will submit to run on all clusters.
                              NOTE: SlurmDBD must up.
      --container             Path to OCI container bundle
      --container-id          OCI container ID
  -m, --distribution=type     distribution method for processes to nodes
                              (type = block|cyclic|arbitrary)
      --mail-type=type        notify on state change: BEGIN, END, FAIL or ALL
      --mail-user=user        who to send email notification for job state
                              changes
      --mcs-label=mcs         mcs label if mcs plugin mcs/group is used
  -n, --ntasks=ntasks         number of tasks to run
      --nice[=value]          decrease scheduling priority by value
      --no-requeue            if set, do not permit the job to be requeued
      --ntasks-per-node=n     number of tasks to invoke on each node
  -N, --nodes=N               number of nodes on which to run (N = min[-max])
      --oom-kill-step[=0|1]   set the OOMKillStep behaviour
  -o, --output=out            file for batch script's standard output
  -O, --overcommit            overcommit resources
  -p, --partition=partition   partition requested
      --parsable              outputs only the jobid and cluster name (if present),
                              separated by semicolon, only on successful submission.
      --power=flags           power management options
      --priority=value        set the priority of the job to value
      --profile=value         enable acct_gather_profile for detailed data
                              value is all or none or any combination of
                              energy, lustre, network or task
      --propagate[=rlimits]   propagate all [or specific list of] rlimits
  -q, --qos=qos               quality of service
  -Q, --quiet                 quiet mode (suppress informational messages)
      --reboot                reboot compute nodes before starting job
      --requeue[=expedited]   if set, permit the job to be requeued
  -s, --oversubscribe         over subscribe resources with other jobs
  -S, --core-spec=cores       count of reserved cores
      --signal=[[R][B]:]num[@time] send signal when time limit within time seconds
      --spread-job            spread job across as many nodes as possible
      --spread-segments       spread job segments across separate base blocks
      --switches=max-switches{@max-time-to-wait}
                              Optimum switches and max time to wait for optimum
      --thread-spec=threads   count of reserved threads
  -t, --time=minutes          time limit
      --time-min=minutes      minimum time limit (if distinct)
      --tres-bind=...         task to tres binding options
      --tres-per-task=list    list of tres required per task
      --uid=user_id           user ID to run job as (user root only)
      --use-min-nodes         if a range of node counts is given, prefer the
                              smaller count
  -v, --verbose               verbose mode (multiple -v's increase verbosity)
  -W, --wait                  wait for completion of submitted job
      --wckey=wckey           wckey to run job under
      --wrap[=command string] wrap command string in a sh script and submit

Constraint options:
      --cluster-constraint=[!]list specify a list of cluster constraints
      --contiguous            demand a contiguous range of nodes
  -C, --constraint=list       specify a list of constraints
  -F, --nodefile=filename     request a specific list of hosts
      --mem=MB                minimum amount of real memory
      --mincpus=n             minimum number of logical processors (threads)
                              per node
      --reservation=name      allocate resources from named reservation
      --tmp=MB                minimum amount of temporary disk
  -w, --nodelist=hosts...     request a specific list of hosts
  -x, --exclude=hosts...      exclude a specific list of hosts

Consumable resources related options:
      --exclusive[=user]      allocate nodes in exclusive mode when
                              cpu consumable resource is enabled
      --exclusive[=mcs]       allocate nodes in exclusive mode when
                              cpu consumable resource is enabled
                              and mcs plugin is enabled
      --mem-per-cpu=MB        maximum amount of real memory per allocated
                              cpu required by the job.
                              --mem >= --mem-per-cpu if --mem is specified.
      --resv-ports            reserve communication ports

Affinity/Multi-core options: (when the task/affinity plugin is enabled)
                              For the following 4 options, you are
                              specifying the minimum resources available for
                              the node(s) allocated to the job.
      --sockets-per-node=S    number of sockets per node to allocate
      --cores-per-socket=C    number of cores per socket to allocate
      --threads-per-core=T    number of threads per core to allocate
  -B, --extra-node-info=S[:C[:T]]  combine request of sockets per node,
                              cores per socket and threads per core.
                              Specify an asterisk (*) as a placeholder,
                              a minimum value, or a min-max range.

      --ntasks-per-core=n     number of tasks to invoke on each core
      --ntasks-per-socket=n   number of tasks to invoke on each socket
      --hint=                 Bind tasks according to application hints
                              (see "--hint=help" for options)
      --mem-bind=             Bind memory to locality domains (ldom)
                              (see "--mem-bind=help" for options)

GPU scheduling options:
      --cpus-per-gpu=n        number of CPUs required per allocated GPU
  -G, --gpus=n                count of GPUs required for the job
      --gpu-bind=...          task to gpu binding options
      --gpu-freq=...          frequency and voltage of GPUs
      --gpus-per-node=n       number of GPUs required per allocated node
      --gpus-per-socket=n     number of GPUs required per allocated socket
      --gpus-per-task=n       number of GPUs required per spawned task
      --mem-per-gpu=n         real memory required per allocated GPU

Help options:
  -h, --help                  show this help message
      --usage                 display brief usage message

Other options:
  -V, --version               output version information and exit

The Slurm cluster will run the application through Singularity. You must convert the initial command to run with Singularity. This means you should:

You must use mpirun as a prefix to the execution. It needs to specify any resource requirements (e.g., nodes and proc mapping, if requested) before the singularity command.
Instead of an execution to the <app> You will next need to do /shared/apps/bin/singularity exec --pwd <pwd> <container> <original command>
Add echo "Start time:" $( date +%s ) before your running command
Add echo "End time:" $( date +%s ) after your running command
You must load the module for openmpi and libfabric-aws

The following application containers MUST be used:
      lammps:  /shared/apps/containers/fractale-agent-experiments_lammps-reax.sif
     amg2023: /shared/apps/containers/fractale-agent-experiments_amg2023.sif
     kripke:  /shared/apps/containers/fractale-agent-experiments_kripke.sif
 all-reduce: /shared/apps/containers/fractale-agent-experiments_osu-allreduce.sif
all-latency: /shared/apps/containers/fractale-agent-experiments_osu-latency.sif

The following pwd have application data. If a name is not in this list you do not need --pwd
      lammps:  /opt/lammps-reax
inputs.script: flux submit -N1 -n 64 lmp -v x 20 -v y 20 -v z 20 -in in.reaxff.hns

The use of the specified AWS EFA-enabled fabric via the 'libfabric-aws' module is critical for achieving low-latency communication, which is essential for this type of simulation.
outputs.jobspec:
#!/bin/bash

# Job Details
#SBATCH --job-name=lammps_reaxff  # A descriptive name for your job
#SBATCH --output=lammps_%j.out   # Standard output file
#SBATCH --error=lammps_%j.err    # Standard error file

# Resource Allocation
# We are requesting 1 full node, with 64 tasks. This matches the original flux command.
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=64
#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=64 # Ensures all 64 tasks are placed on the single node

# Performance Optimizations
# --exclusive ensures that this job has the entire node to itself, preventing
# interference from other jobs, which is crucial for performance-sensitive HPC tasks.
#SBATCH --exclusive

# By binding tasks to specific CPU cores, we can improve performance by reducing
# context switching and improving cache utilization.
#SBATCH --cpu-bind=cores

# Load necessary modules for MPI and networking
# OpenMPI is required for mpirun, and libfabric-aws is needed for EFA support.
echo "Loading modules..."
module load openmpi
module load libfabric-aws

# Start timer
echo "Start time:" $(date +%s)

# Run the LAMMPS simulation using mpirun and Singularity
# -np 64 specifies the number of processes for MPI.
# The singularity exec command runs the lmp executable from within the container.
# --pwd sets the working directory inside the container to where the input data is located.
echo "Running LAMMPS simulation..."
mpirun -np 64 singularity exec --pwd /opt/lammps-reax /shared/apps/containers/fractale-agent-experiments_lammps-reax.sif lmp -v x 20 -v y 20 -v z 20 -in in.reaxff.hns

# End timer
echo "End time:" $(date +%s)

echo "Job finished."

#!/bin/bash

# We are requesting 192 total MPI tasks, directly translating the -n 192 from the flux command.

# For performance, we explicitly state how many tasks to place on each node.
# This ensures an even distribution (192 tasks / 3 nodes = 64 tasks/node).

# This flag is added for performance. It ensures that our job gets exclusive access to the nodes,
# preventing other jobs from running on them and interfering with performance.

# It is good practice to specify an error file for stderr, with the job ID (%j).

# openmpi is required for mpirun

module load openmpi
module load libfabric-aws

#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --nodes=4
#SBATCH --ntasks=256
#SBATCH --job-name=lammps_reaxff
#SBATCH --output=lammps_reaxff_%j.out
#SBATCH --error=lammps_reaxff_%j.err

# Performance-related directives
# Distribute tasks evenly across nodes (256 tasks / 4 nodes = 64 tasks/node).
# This is a good starting point as hpc7g.6xlarge instances have 64 vCPUs, mapping one task per vCPU.
#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=64

# Ensure exclusive access to the nodes for best performance.
#SBATCH --exclusive

# This setting can improve performance by affecting how MPI ranks are placed onto physical hardware.
# Cyclic distribution can be beneficial for communication-intensive applications.
#SBATCH --distribution=cyclic:cyclic

# Load necessary modules for MPI and high-performance networking on AWS.
module load openmpi
module load libfabric-aws

# Record start time for benchmarking.
echo "Start time:" $( date +%s )

# Execute the LAMMPS simulation within a Singularity container.
# mpirun from the loaded OpenMPI module launches the parallel job.
# The singularity exec command runs the application from the specified container image.
# --pwd sets the working directory inside the container to where the input data is located.
mpirun singularity exec --pwd /opt/lammps-reax /shared/apps/containers/fractale-agent-experiments_lammps-reax.sif lmp -v x 20 -v y 20 -v z 20 -in in.reaxff.hns

# Record end time for benchmarking.
echo "End time:" $( date +%s )

#!/bin/bash

# SBATCH DIRECTIVES
#--------------------

# Set the name of the job for identification
#SBATCH --job-name=lammps

# Request 5 nodes for this job
#SBATCH --nodes=5

# Request a total of 320 tasks (MPI processes)
#SBATCH --ntasks=320

# Calculate and specify tasks per node (320 tasks / 5 nodes = 64)
# This helps the scheduler optimize placement and can improve performance.
#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=64

# Request exclusive access to the nodes. This is a key performance enhancement
# as it prevents other jobs from running on the same nodes and causing contention
# for CPU, memory, or network resources.
#SBATCH --exclusive

# Define output and error file names, using the job ID (%j) for uniqueness
#SBATCH --output=lammps-%j.out
#SBATCH --error=lammps-%j.err

#--------------------
# JOB SCRIPT
#--------------------

# Load the required modules for OpenMPI and AWS EFA networking
echo "Loading modules..."
module load openmpi libfabric-aws

# Echo start time for basic profiling
echo "Start time:" $( date +%s )

# Execute the LAMMPS simulation.
# 'mpirun' starts the parallel job across the allocated resources.
# 'singularity exec' runs the command within the specified container.
# The '--pwd' flag sets the correct working directory inside the container for LAMMPS.
echo "Starting LAMMPS simulation via Singularity..."
mpirun singularity exec --pwd /opt/lammps-reax /shared/apps/containers/fractale-agent-experiments_lammps-reax.sif lmp -v x 20 -v y 20 -v z 20 -in in.reaxff.hns

# Echo end time for basic profiling
echo "End time:" $( date +%s )

#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=lammps_reaxff
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=64
#SBATCH --output=lammps_output_%j.log
#SBATCH --error=lammps_error_%j.log

# Performance Enhancement: Bind each task to a specific CPU core.
# This prevents the operating system from migrating tasks between cores, which
# improves cache utilization and overall performance. This is a more explicit
# and robust way to achieve the goal of Flux's '--cpu-affinity=per-task'.
#SBATCH --cpu-bind=cores

# Performance Enhancement: Request exclusive access to the node.
# This ensures no other jobs run on the node, guaranteeing all resources
# (memory bandwidth, network, etc.) are available to this job.
#SBATCH --exclusive

module load openmpi
module load libfabric-aws

echo "Start time:" $( date +%s )

# mpirun is used to launch the parallel application, and Slurm's process
# manager will automatically provide it with the correct number of tasks and hosts.
# The '--pwd' flag sets the working directory inside the container to where the input data is located.
mpirun /shared/apps/bin/singularity exec --pwd /opt/lammps-reax /shared/apps/containers/fractale-agent-experiments_lammps-reax.sif lmp -v x 20 -v y 20 -v z 20 -in in.reaxff.hns

echo "End time:" $( date +%s )

#!/bin/bash

#SBATCH --nodes=2
#SBATCH --ntasks=128
# This was derived from the -N2 and -n128 flags in the flux command.

#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=64
# We have 128 tasks on 2 nodes, so we explicitly set 64 tasks per node.

#SBATCH --job-name=lammps_reaxff
# A descriptive name for the job.

#SBATCH --output=lammps_reaxff.out
#SBATCH --error=lammps_reaxff.err
# Specifying output and error files.

#SBATCH --exclusive
# This ensures the job gets exclusive access to the nodes, which is crucial for performance-sensitive MPI applications.

#SBATCH --cpu-bind=cores
# This binds each task to a physical core, which is the Slurm equivalent of flux's cpu-affinity=per-task and is optimal for performance.

#SBATCH --distribution=cyclic:cyclic
# This ensures that tasks are distributed cyclically across sockets and then nodes, which can improve performance by balancing the communication load.

# Load necessary modules for MPI and high-speed networking
module load openmpi
module load libfabric-aws

# Start timing
echo "Start time:" $( date +%s )

# Execute the lammps command within a Singularity container using mpirun
# The container and its path are specified as per the instructions.
# --pwd sets the working directory inside the container.
mpirun /shared/apps/bin/singularity exec --pwd /opt/lammps-reax /shared/apps/containers/fractale-agent-experiments_lammps-reax.sif lmp -v x 20 -v y 20 -v z 20 -in in.reaxff.hns

#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --nodes=4
#SBATCH --ntasks=256
#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=64
#SBATCH --job-name=lammps
#SBATCH --output=slurm-%j.out
#SBATCH --error=slurm-%j.err

# This directive pins each MPI task to a physical CPU core.
# This is the Slurm equivalent of the flux '-o cpu-affinity=per-task' option and helps
# prevent tasks from migrating between cores, which can improve performance and reproducibility.
#SBATCH --cpu-bind=cores

# Load the required modules for MPI and the AWS Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA)
module load openmpi libfabric-aws

# Record the start time for benchmarking
echo "Start time:" $( date +%s )

# Execute the LAMMPS simulation using mpirun and Singularity.
# mpirun will automatically pick up the node and task counts from Slurm.
# Singularity runs the application in a containerized environment.
# The --pwd flag sets the working directory inside the container to where the input data is located.
mpirun /shared/apps/bin/singularity exec --pwd /opt/lammps-reax /shared/apps/containers/fractale-agent-experiments_lammps-reax.sif lmp -v x 20 -v y 20 -v z 20 -in in.reaxff.hns

# Record the end time for benchmarking
echo "End time:" $( date +%s )

#!/bin/bash

# Slurm job directives
# These settings are derived from the original Flux command: -N5 -n 320
#SBATCH --nodes=5
#SBATCH --ntasks=320
#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=64
#SBATCH --job-name=lammps_reaxff
#SBATCH --output=lammps_%j.out
#SBATCH --error=lammps_%j.err

# --- Performance-related options ---
# --exclusive: This is a key performance enhancement. It ensures that our job gets exclusive
# access to the allocated nodes, preventing any other jobs from running on them and
# causing resource contention (CPU, memory, network), which leads to more consistent performance.
#SBATCH --exclusive

# --- Environment Setup ---
# Load the necessary modules. openmpi is required for mpirun, and libfabric-aws
# is essential for enabling high-speed networking with AWS Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA).
echo "Loading modules..."
module load openmpi
module load libfabric-aws

# --- Execution ---
# Record the start time for benchmarking.
echo "Start time:" $( date +%s )

echo "Running LAMMPS simulation..."
# We use mpirun to launch the parallel application across the allocated nodes.
# --bind-to core: This option is the Slurm/OpenMPI equivalent of the original Flux
# '-o cpu-affinity=per-task'. It pins each MPI process to a specific CPU core.
# This is crucial for performance as it prevents the operating system from moving
# tasks between cores, which would invalidate caches and decrease performance.
# The rest of the command executes the lmp binary within the specified Singularity container.
mpirun --bind-to core \
    /shared/apps/bin/singularity exec --pwd /opt/lammps-reax \
    /shared/apps/containers/fractale-agent-experiments_lammps-reax.sif \
    lmp -v x 20 -v y 20 -v z 20 -in in.reaxff.hns

# Record the end time for benchmarking.
echo "End time:" $( date +%s )

echo "Job finished."

#!/bin/bash
#
# Slurm batch script for running the AMG benchmark
#

# -- Directives specifying resource requirements --

#SBATCH --nodes=2
# This requests 2 compute nodes, same as the `-N2` in the original flux command.

#SBATCH --ntasks=128
# This requests a total of 128 MPI tasks, same as `-n 128` in flux.

#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=64
# For optimal performance, we specify the number of tasks per node.
# hpc7g.6xlarge instances have 64 cores, so this maps one task to each physical core.

#SBATCH --job-name=amg_benchmark
# It is good practice to give the job a descriptive name.

#SBATCH --output=amg_job_%j.out
# Redirect standard output to a file named after the job ID.

#SBATCH --error=amg_job_%j.err
# Redirect standard error to a file named after the job ID.

# -- Performance-related Directives --

#SBATCH --exclusive
# This ensures that no other jobs will run on the allocated nodes, preventing resource contention.

#SBATCH --distribution=cyclic:cyclic
# This distributes tasks in a round-robin fashion across nodes and then cores.
# It can help ensure that memory access patterns are balanced, improving performance.


# --- Job Execution --- 

# 1. Load necessary modules
# The openmpi module provides the mpirun command and Slurm integration.
# The libfabric-aws module is crucial for high-speed networking with EFA.
echo "Loading modules..."
module load openmpi
module load libfabric-aws

# 2. Run the application
echo "Starting job execution..."

echo "Start time:" $( date +%s )

# mpirun launches the application across the allocated resources.
# The command is executed within the specified Singularity container.
mpirun -np 128 /shared/apps/bin/singularity exec /shared/apps/containers/fractale-agent-experiments_amg2023.sif amg -problem 2 -n 90 90 90 -P 4 8 4

echo "End time:" $( date +%s )

echo "Job finished."

# This is the name of the job, useful for tracking.

#SBATCH --nodes=4
# We are requesting 4 nodes, same as the -N4 from the flux command.

#SBATCH --ntasks=256
# We are requesting 256 total MPI tasks, same as the -n 256 from the flux command.

#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=64
# To improve performance and ensure even distribution, we specify 64 tasks per node (256 tasks / 4 nodes).

#SBATCH --exclusive
# This flag is added to ensure that our job has exclusive access to the allocated nodes,
# preventing other jobs from interfering and ensuring consistent performance.

# Load necessary modules for MPI and the high-speed network fabric.
module load openmpi
module load libfabric-aws

# Echo start time for logging purposes.
echo "Start time:" $( date +%s )

# The mpirun command launches the parallel application.
# It automatically picks up the number of nodes and tasks from the Slurm environment.
# We then execute the application inside a Singularity container.
mpirun /shared/apps/bin/singularity exec /shared/apps/containers/fractale-agent-experiments_amg2023.sif amg -problem 2 -n 90 90 90 -P 4 8 8

# Echo end time for logging purposes.
echo "End time:" $( date +%s )

# improvement that binds each task to a specific CPU core. This can improve performance by
# increasing cache efficiency and reducing context switching.

module load openmpi

# -npernode 64: Explicitly tells OpenMPI how many processes to launch on each node.
# The rest of the command executes the amg application within the specified Singularity container.
mpirun -np 128 --bind-to core -npernode 64 \
/shared/apps/bin/singularity exec \
/shared/apps/containers/fractale-agent-experiments_amg2023.sif \
amg -problem 2 -n 90 90 90 -P 4 8 4

# is essential for enabling high-speed networking with AWS Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA).

module load openmpi
module load libfabric-aws

# --- Execution ---
# Record the start time for benchmarking.
echo "Start time:" $( date +%s )

echo "Running LAMMPS simulation..."
# We use mpirun to launch the parallel application across the allocated nodes.
# --bind-to core: This option is the Slurm/OpenMPI equivalent of the original Flux
# '-o cpu-affinity=per-task'. It pins each MPI process to a specific CPU core.
# This is crucial for performance as it prevents the operating system from moving
# tasks between cores, which would invalidate caches and decrease performance.
# The rest of the command executes the lmp binary within the specified Singularity container.
mpirun --bind-to core \
    /shared/apps/bin/singularity exec --pwd /opt/lammps-reax \
    /shared/apps/containers/fractale-agent-experiments_lammps-reax.sif \
    lmp -v x 20 -v y 20 -v z 20 -in in.reaxff.hns

# Record the end time for benchmarking.
echo "End time:" $( date +%s )
